title: Distance of the discrete derivative from low degree
statement: Let $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ be a Boolean function that is $\varepsilon$-far from degree $\le d$, where $d \ge 2$; in particular $0 \le \varepsilon \le 1$. For a shift $h \in \{0,1\}^n$, write $\partial_h f$ for the discrete derivative $\partial_h f(x) = f(x) \oplus f(x \oplus h)$. Then there exists a real number $\delta \ge \varepsilon$ such that for every $h \in \{0,1\}^n$ there is a Boolean function $g : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ for which, if $g$ has degree $\le d-1$, then $\dist(\partial_h f, g) \ge \delta$.
hypotheses_covered: f is a Boolean function on {0,1}^n
f is ε-far from degree ≤ d (which includes 0 ≤ ε ≤ 1)
replaced:
If $d \ge 2$ and $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ is $\varepsilon$-far from degree
$\le d$, then there exists $\delta \ge \varepsilon$ such that for every
$h \in \{0,1\}^n$ there exists a Boolean function $g$ of degree $\le d{-}1$
with $\dist(\Delta_h f, g) \ge \delta$.  Intuitively, the multiplicative derivative
$\Delta_h f(x) = f(x) \oplus f(x \oplus h)$ is on average far from degree
$\le d{-}1$.
